title: An Atypical Presentation of Pyridoxine-Dependent Epilepsy Diagnosed with Whole Exome Sequencing and Treated with Lysine Restriction and Supplementation with Arginine and Pyridoxine
case_prompt:
A 3-day-old male infant was born at term to a nonconsanguineous Caucasian couple after an uncomplicated pregnancy. He presented with increased work of breathing, grunting, intercostal retractions, and an axillary temperature of 104°F. Shortly thereafter, multiple episodes of apnea and desaturation occurred, some accompanied by arching and abnormal eye movements concerning for seizures. 

A sepsis evaluation was performed, and empiric therapy with ampicillin, gentamicin, and acyclovir was started; all cultures remained negative. On day of life (DOL) 4, cerebrospinal fluid lactate was 4.2 mmol/L (normal 1.1–2.8) and whole-blood lactate was 6.3 mmol/L (normal 0.5–2.0); ammonia was 58 μmol/L (normal 0–75). Urine organic acids showed moderately increased lactate and elevations of 2-hydroxyisovalerate, 4-hydroxyphenyllactate, and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate. An acylcarnitine profile was normal, but free carnitine was 7 μmol/L (normal 10–21) and total carnitine was 13.8 μmol/L (normal 17–41). Plasma amino acids revealed citrulline 5 μmol/L (normal 10–34), glutamine 713 μmol/L (normal 337–673), and an alanine-to-lysine ratio of 4.4.

An echocardiogram on DOL 4 showed moderately diminished left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 45.2%) and mildly diminished right ventricular function. Concerned about a mitochondrial disorder, the infant was started on biotin, thiamine, and riboflavin, and rapid genetic testing was sent.

An electroencephalogram on DOL 4 demonstrated multifocal seizures; phenobarbital, levetiracetam, and caffeine were initiated. Brain ultrasound on DOL 4 was unremarkable. Continuous EEG on DOL 5 showed burst-suppression with epileptiform activity, prompting intubation. Brain MRI on DOL 5 revealed mild diffuse thinning of the corpus callosum. Despite phenobarbital and levetiracetam, seizures persisted on DOL 6, and fosphenytoin and midazolam were added. Over the next days, seizures resolved, and by DOL 11 the infant was weaned off fosphenytoin and midazolam and extubated. A repeat echocardiogram on DOL 5 had normalized.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Mitochondrial disorder was considered because of lactic acidosis, seizures, and depressed cardiac function — “Due to concerns for a mitochondrial disorder in the setting of lactic acidosis, seizures, and depressed cardiac function, the patient was started on biotin, thiamine, and riboflavin.”  
2. Infectious process was in the differential given fever and respiratory distress, but was unlikely as cultures remained negative and these symptoms resolved with seizure control — “The fever and respiratory distress may have reflected an infectious process that was not elucidated on cultures, though these symptoms resolved as the seizures resolved.”  
3. Inborn errors of metabolism were suspected based on the elevated lactate and abnormal urine organic acids, but normal acylcarnitine profile and specific amino acid patterns did not fit a single known metabolic disorder — “The differential diagnosis was initially wide and included mitochondrial disorders, infectious processes, inborn errors of metabolism, and other single-gene etiologies for infantile seizures.”  
4. Other single-gene epilepsies were considered, but an initial response to multiple antiepileptic drugs and the lack of a classic pyridoxine trial made pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy less apparent early on — “In our patient, because seizures initially responded to multiple AEDs and comorbidities including cardiac dysfunction somewhat obscured the diagnosis, a pyridoxine trial was deferred.”  
5. Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy was confirmed by rapid genetic testing revealing the causative variant — “On day of life 12, whole exome sequencing results revealed a homozygous pathogenic variant in ALDH7A1: c.1279G > C (p.E427Q).”
